distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer disease leaf for the full clinical spectrum of cyanide poisoning across inhalational smoke exposure, industrial or laboratory exposure, ingestion of cyanide salts or cyanogenic materials, nitroprusside-related toxicity, dermal or inhaled nitrile contexts, rapid cardiovascular collapse, seizures, coma, severe lactic acidosis, and antidote/supportive-care contexts.
distillation_scope.boundary_policy: Smoke inhalation, carbon monoxide coexposure, thermal airway injury, burn trauma, intentional ingestion, occupational exposure, nitroprusside infusion, and severe poisoning are represented as exposure/source/context axes, event hazards, risk modifiers, or treatment modifiers. They are not disease-name qualifiers and do not collapse this manifold into carbon monoxide poisoning.
distillation_scope.case_separation_note: This distillation was created from the disease name only and without searching, reading, or structuring real cyanide poisoning cases.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Cyanide exposure and absorbed body burden
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Hidden absorbed cyanide load across smoke inhalation, enclosed fires, industrial or laboratory salts, ingestion, cyanogenic plant or nitrile exposure, dermal/inhalational occupational exposure, or nitroprusside-derived cyanide generation. It gates onset speed, blood cyanide when available, and all downstream toxic physiology.
Cyanide binds the ferric iron of cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV), blocks oxidative phosphorylation, and prevents mitochondrial oxygen utilization despite oxygen delivery to tissues.
Cells cannot use delivered oxygen, producing high venous oxygen saturation and low arteriovenous oxygen difference when measured, with rapid transition to global cellular energy failure.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Severe lactic acidosis from anaerobic metabolism
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Blocked oxidative phosphorylation forces anaerobic glycolysis and lactate generation. Marked lactate elevation and acidemia are central likelihood and severity axes, especially when disproportionate to measured hypoxemia or COHb.
Brain ATP failure causes headache, dizziness, agitation, altered mental status, syncope, seizures, coma, respiratory drive failure, and hypoxic-ischemic brain injury risk.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Myocardial energy failure and circulatory collapse
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Myocardial mitochondrial poisoning, profound acidosis, catecholamine stress, and tissue hypoxia drive tachycardia followed by hypotension, dysrhythmia, shock, cardiac arrest, and short-term death hazard.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Smoke co-toxin and airway injury context
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Fire smoke can deliver cyanide from combustion of nitrogen-containing materials while simultaneously adding carbon monoxide exposure, airway thermal injury, bronchospasm, pulmonary edema, burns, and trauma. This context modifies respiratory and oxygen-delivery hazards without redefining cyanide poisoning as CO poisoning.

Endogenous sulfur-donor availability, hepatic mitochondrial rhodanese activity, renal thiocyanate clearance, nitroprusside cyanide generation rate, and antidote access determine whether cyanide can be converted to thiocyanate fast enough to avoid persistent toxicity.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Accumulated hypoxic, acidemic, seizure, and shock injury
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Irreversible injury accumulates during untreated histotoxic hypoxia, severe acidemia, seizures, respiratory failure, shock, or cardiac arrest. This mechanism explains residual hazard after the cyanide-binding mechanism is suppressed.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: A compatible cyanide exposure context is the upstream evidence for absorbed body burden.
Source documentation, co-exposed persons, container evidence, workplace context, or toxicology history raises the probability that the exposure is cyanide-specific.
Dose, concentration, duration, enclosed space, and respiratory minute ventilation determine absorbed burden.
Even short untreated intervals can accumulate irreversible hypoxic and shock injury in severe cyanide poisoning.
Smoke inhalation is a common cyanide exposure context and adds airway injury and carbon monoxide coexposure possibilities.
Enclosed structure fires with synthetic material combustion raise cyanide and CO co-toxin burden.
High-dose or prolonged nitroprusside can generate cyanide faster than detoxification and thiocyanate clearance can compensate.
Blood cyanide is direct body-burden evidence when measured, but sampling and availability often lag clinical decisions.
Absorbed cyanide rapidly binds mitochondrial complex IV.
Insufficient sulfur-donor detoxification or impaired clearance permits active cyanide to persist.
Complex IV blockade prevents cellular oxygen extraction and oxidative phosphorylation.
Venous oxygen saturation can be abnormally high because tissues cannot extract oxygen.
Oxygen extraction failure lowers the arteriovenous oxygen saturation difference when paired samples are available.
High venous oxyhemoglobin can make venous blood appear unusually bright red, although this sign is insensitive.
Mitochondrial respiration blockade forces anaerobic metabolism and lactate generation.
Marked lactate elevation is the most useful widely available biochemical signature of severe cyanide physiology.
Lactic acidemia lowers arterial pH.
Buffer consumption lowers serum bicarbonate.
Lactate is a major unmeasured anion in severe cyanide poisoning.
Metabolic acidosis can produce deep compensatory tachypnea before respiratory collapse.
Acidemia increases ventilatory drive when CNS and muscle reserve remain intact.

Severe acidemia worsens neuronal dysfunction and seizure risk.

Profound acidemia depresses myocardium and worsens vasoplegia and arrhythmia risk.
Early sympathetic response often causes tachycardia; terminal poisoning may cause bradycardia or pulseless rhythm.
Circulatory failure manifests as hypotension.
Shock lowers MAP and accelerates organ injury.
Mitochondrial myocardial failure and acidemia raise collapse risk.
Acidemia, myocardial hypoxia, and catecholamine stress increase dysrhythmia risk.

Severe myocardial energy failure and shock can cause myocardial injury.
Combustion smoke often contains both cyanide and carbon monoxide.
COHb quantifies carbon monoxide coexposure, which modifies oxygen delivery but is not cyanide itself.
Thermal and chemical airway injury can coexist with cyanide physiology.
Airway edema, bronchospasm, pulmonary injury, coma, and acidosis can converge on respiratory failure.
Shock, arrest, rhabdomyolysis, and antidote-related thiocyanate burden can contribute to AKI risk.

Shock and cardiac arrest are the dominant immediate lethal pathway.
Coma, seizures, loss of airway protection, and central respiratory failure raise death hazard.

Toxic ingestion is a source-context signal that becomes cyanide-specific when paired with cyanide access or systemic asphyxiant physiology.
The combined syndrome of preserved oxygen delivery with cellular oxygen-use failure is a systemic asphyxiant toxidrome.
Impaired tissue oxygen extraction can preserve oxyhemoglobin-rich coloration, producing a bright red appearance in some severe cases.
Soot on the face, mouth, or airway is a physical marker of smoke exposure context.
Smoke inhalation often produces carbon monoxide coexposure alongside cyanide exposure.
Coma, seizure, and central respiratory drive failure can produce acute respiratory failure.

Deep coma and loss of airway protection often require intubation and ventilation.

Severe CNS energy failure can trigger generalized tonic-clonic seizures.
Blood pressure may initially be preserved or catecholamine-elevated but falls with cyanide circulatory collapse.

Smoke injury and respiratory failure can lower measured blood-gas oxygen saturation.

axes.clinical_meaning: Any credible cyanide source context, including smoke inhalation, industrial/lab exposure, ingestion, cyanogenic materials, nitriles, or nitroprusside.
Probability that the observed exposure context specifically involved cyanide rather than a nonspecific toxic exposure.
Composite of concentration, dose, enclosed-space duration, respiratory minute ventilation, dermal area, or infusion generation rate.
Elapsed time from last plausible cyanide exposure or start of high-risk infusion to medical assessment or antidote.
Exposure to fire smoke or combustion products that can contain cyanide, carbon monoxide, particulates, and airway irritants.
Enclosed structure or vehicle fire exposure, especially with synthetic nitrogen-containing material combustion.
Occupational or laboratory access to cyanide salts, electroplating, mining, metal processing, chemical synthesis, or similar settings.
Known or suspected ingestion of cyanide salt, contaminated substance, or capsule/powder/liquid with cyanide access.

axes.display_name: Cyanogenic plant or nitrile exposure context
axes.clinical_meaning: Cassava or other cyanogenic glycoside context, acetonitrile or nitrile exposure, or other delayed cyanide-generating exposure.
Sodium nitroprusside use with potential cyanide generation, especially high dose, prolonged infusion, renal/hepatic dysfunction, or limited thiosulfate reserve.
Direct blood cyanide concentration when available; useful retrospectively but often not rapidly available enough for acute treatment decisions.
Thiocyanate reflects cyanide detoxification and can accumulate during nitroprusside exposure, thiosulfate therapy, or renal impairment.
Probability that the same smoke exposure also caused carbon monoxide poisoning physiology; kept as context rather than folded into cyanide identity.
Measured COHb quantifies carbon monoxide coexposure in smoke cases and modifies oxygen-delivery reserve; it does not diagnose cyanide itself.
Methemoglobin level is usually baseline unless nitrite donors are used or another oxidant is present; it creates a cyanide sink but reduces oxygen-carrying capacity.
ScvO2 or mixed venous oxygen saturation may be high in histotoxic hypoxia because tissues cannot extract oxygen.
Difference between arterial and venous oxygen saturation; may be abnormally low in oxygen extraction failure.
Unusually bright venous blood appearance from high venous oxyhemoglobin; insensitive and not required.
Markedly elevated lactate from histotoxic hypoxia; severe cyanide physiology often produces rapid, high lactate out of proportion to routine hypoxemia measures.
Arterial pH decreases with lactic acidosis and respiratory failure.
Bicarbonate falls with lactic acid buffer consumption.
Anion gap rises with lactic acidosis.
Deep tachypneic respiratory compensation for severe metabolic acidosis when respiratory drive is preserved.
Pulse oximetry may be normal in pure cyanide histotoxic hypoxia; low values suggest smoke lung injury, respiratory failure, shock, or coexisting oxygen-delivery pathology.
Acidemia can produce tachypnea, but coma, seizure, apnea, or arrest can cause a low respiratory rate.
Cyanide poisoning can cause early tachycardia, preserved pulse, bradycardia near arrest, or pulseless rhythms depending on phase.
Clinically significant low blood pressure from cardiovascular collapse.
MAP falls in shock and directly affects perfusion support needs.
Clinical shock with hypotension, poor perfusion, vasopressor need, arrest physiology, or severe lactate/hypoperfusion context.
Severity of shock, integrating vasopressor requirement, hypotension depth, perfusion markers, and arrest proximity.
Myocardial injury marker after severe cyanide-related shock, hypoxia, acidosis, or arrest.
Early or mild CNS symptom; often absent in fulminant collapse.
Early nonspecific CNS symptom from histotoxic hypoxia.
Nonspecific early toxic symptom or ingestion/smoke-related symptom.
Nonspecific toxic or ingestion-associated symptom; also modifies aspiration risk in coma.
Subjective breathlessness from acidosis, smoke inhalation, airway injury, pulmonary edema, or panic during exposure.
Soot, facial/oropharyngeal burns, hoarseness, stridor, bronchospasm, or airway edema suggesting thermal/chemical airway injury.
Agitation, confusion, somnolence, coma, or other altered consciousness from CNS energy failure.
Depth of encephalopathy from mild confusion to unresponsive coma.
Structured consciousness score; lower values indicate deeper coma and airway risk.
Severity of coma as a child phenotype of altered mental status.
Transient loss of consciousness from CNS energy failure, dysrhythmia, or shock.
Generalized or focal seizure from CNS energy failure or severe acidemia.
Severity, recurrence, or status-epilepticus-like burden of seizure activity.
Risk of recurrent seizure or status epilepticus during active poisoning.
Risk of structural brain injury after prolonged coma, seizure, shock, or cardiac arrest.
Risk of needing ventilatory support from coma, seizure, acidosis, smoke inhalation, airway edema, pulmonary edema, or arrest.
Risk of rapid progression to severe shock or refractory hypotension.
Risk of clinically significant dysrhythmia during cyanide-related acidemia, myocardial hypoxia, shock, or antidote/toxin context.
Risk of cardiac arrest from severe mitochondrial poisoning, acidemia, hypoxia, and shock.
Risk of AKI after shock/arrest, rhabdomyolysis, smoke injury, or thiocyanate accumulation context.
Renal function measurement used to track AKI after shock/arrest, smoke injury, nitroprusside/thiocyanate context, or assay interference context.
Risk of pneumothorax or ventilator-associated pressure injury during positive-pressure ventilation.
Availability and feasibility of prompt hydroxocobalamin administration.
Availability and feasibility of sodium thiosulfate as sulfur-donor therapy.

Probability that nitrite-donor methemoglobin induction can be tolerated without unacceptable oxygen-delivery harm; reduced by smoke/CO coexposure, anemia, severe hypoxemia, hypotension, pregnancy, or cardiovascular disease.
Delay until any cyanide-specific antidote can be delivered.
Risk context for thiocyanate accumulation during nitroprusside exposure or thiosulfate therapy, especially with renal impairment.

Lifespan outcome hazard emerging from cyanide body burden, cytochrome oxidase inhibition, histotoxic hypoxia, severe lactic acidosis, coma/seizure, cardiovascular collapse, respiratory failure, arrest, treatment delay, and accumulated injury.
Occupational or laboratory chemical exposure context that can include cyanide salts, electroplating tanks, metal processing, or laboratory access.
Measured or reported ambient cyanide concentration in workplace, enclosed fire, or hazardous-material settings.
Duration of plausible cyanide exposure; longer exposure increases absorbed dose unless ventilation and removal are rapid.
Known or suspected ingestion of a toxic substance; for cyanide this becomes more specific when paired with cyanide salt access, powder/capsule evidence, or systemic asphyxiant physiology.

Clinical toxidrome of cellular oxygen-utilization failure with coma, respiratory failure or gasping, cardiovascular collapse, severe lactate/acidemia, and relatively preserved pulse oximetry when oxygen delivery is not the primary problem.
Bright red or cherry-red skin or mucosal color from high oxyhemoglobin or impaired extraction; insensitive but recognized in severe cyanide and other asphyxiant poisonings.

axes.display_name: Soot on airway, mouth, or face
axes.clinical_meaning: Soot on face, mouth, nares, or airway supporting smoke inhalation and possible cyanide plus carbon monoxide coexposure.
Respiratory failure from coma, apnea, seizure, arrest, smoke airway injury, severe acidemia, or ventilatory collapse during cyanide poisoning.
Absent spontaneous respiration from coma, arrest, seizure, or terminal respiratory drive failure.
Endotracheal intubation and invasive ventilation needed because of coma, apnea, seizure, arrest, smoke airway injury, or severe acidemia.
Metabolic acidosis, usually lactic, from mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation failure.
Severity of metabolic acidosis integrating pH, bicarbonate, base excess, anion gap, and lactate.
Arterial carbon dioxide tension; severe metabolic acidosis can drive very low pCO2 if ventilation is preserved, while coma or arrest can raise it.
Base excess becomes strongly negative in severe lactic metabolic acidosis.
Generalized seizure phenotype from severe CNS energy failure and acidemia.
Systolic blood pressure may be normal early, high from catecholamine stress, or low during cyanide-related circulatory collapse.
Diastolic blood pressure can be preserved early or fall with shock; values must be interpreted with the timing of collapse.
Carbon monoxide exposure commonly co-occurs in smoke inhalation cases and modifies oxygen delivery without replacing cyanide physiology.
Methemoglobin percent is usually low before nitrite therapy in cyanide poisoning; elevation suggests nitrite treatment or another oxidant context.
Blood gas oxygen saturation may be preserved in pure histotoxic hypoxia but can be low during arrest, smoke inhalation, respiratory failure, or sampling from venous/mixed blood.
Body temperature is variable in cyanide poisoning and may be low after collapse or normal unless smoke injury, seizure, or coexisting exposure modifies it.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: High lactate is a severity marker and residual driver of short-term death hazard.
Lower pH increases dysrhythmia risk and myocardial instability.
Severe acidemia depresses myocardial and neurologic function and raises mortality hazard.
The combination of high venous oxygen saturation with high lactate reflects oxygen extraction failure rather than simple oxygen delivery failure.
Low arteriovenous oxygen extraction with rising lactate supports histotoxic hypoxia.
Shock compounds histotoxic lactate generation through hypoperfusion.
Lower MAP increases short-term death hazard through perfusion collapse.
Seizures increase brain oxygen demand and worsen injury risk during mitochondrial poisoning.
Respiratory failure adds oxygen-delivery failure, aspiration risk, and ventilatory instability to cyanide physiology.
Cardiac arrest is the most direct terminal event chain.
Smoke exposure adds airway edema, bronchospasm, inhalational lung injury, and burn context.
COHb lowers oxygen-carrying reserve, making methemoglobin induction less tolerable.
Excess methemoglobin can worsen oxygen delivery, especially in smoke inhalation, anemia, or respiratory failure.

treatments.therapeutic_intent: Stop ongoing cyanide absorption or generation and protect rescuers.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Stopping or reducing nitroprusside removes ongoing cyanide generation.
Contaminated clothing, skin, or environment can continue exposure and threaten responders.

treatments.context_specific_role: Upstream exposure control; it cannot reverse already-bound cyanide fast enough when severe physiology is active.

treatments.therapeutic_intent: Maximize oxygen delivery, support ventilation, and manage smoke airway injury while antidote therapy addresses mitochondrial poisoning.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Airway edema, soot, stridor, or burns increase the value of early airway control.
Coma increases aspiration and hypoventilation risk.

side_effects.interpretation: Positive-pressure ventilation can add barotrauma risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Supportive oxygen and airway intervention; it is especially important in smoke inhalation or coma, but cyanide-specific detoxification still requires antidote mechanisms.

treatments.therapeutic_intent: Bind free cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, lowering mitochondrial complex IV inhibition without intentionally impairing oxygen-carrying capacity.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: No pharmacologic effect occurs until the antidote can be administered.
Delayed therapy can bind cyanide but cannot erase completed arrest or hypoxic brain injury.
Marked lactic acidosis is a strong marker of active cyanide physiology.

side_effects.interpretation: Chromophore can interfere with some laboratory assays; true renal effects are uncommon but reported.

treatments.context_specific_role: Cyanide-binding antidote particularly compatible with smoke inhalation because it does not require therapeutic methemoglobinemia.

treatments.therapeutic_intent: Provide sulfur donor substrate for rhodanese-mediated conversion of cyanide to thiocyanate.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Sulfur-donor effect requires drug availability.
Renal impairment increases thiocyanate accumulation risk, especially after repeated dosing or nitroprusside exposure.

side_effects.interpretation: Hypotension can occur, especially with rapid administration or severe baseline shock.
Thiocyanate rises as detoxification product and can accumulate with renal impairment.

treatments.context_specific_role: Sulfur-donor detoxification support; effect is slower than direct cyanide binding and shaped by renal thiocyanate clearance.

treatments.therapeutic_intent: Generate methemoglobin as an alternate cyanide binding sink, while balancing oxygen-carrying capacity, hypotension, and smoke/CO coexposure risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Low oxygen reserve, smoke/CO coexposure, anemia, severe hypotension, or pregnancy lowers tolerance for methemoglobinemia.
COHb plus methemoglobin can critically reduce oxygen-carrying capacity.
Excess methemoglobin worsens oxygen delivery and constrains repeat dosing.

side_effects.interpretation: Methemoglobin and co-toxins can lower effective oxygen carriage and pulse oximetry behavior.

treatments.context_specific_role: Methemoglobin-based cyanide sink; context-sensitive because smoke inhalation and CO coexposure can make oxygen-delivery cost clinically important.

treatments.therapeutic_intent: Maintain perfusion while cyanide-specific antidote therapy reverses mitochondrial poisoning.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Perfusion support is most consequential when MAP is low.
Vasopressors do not reverse histotoxic hypoxia; high lactate should keep antidote urgency active.

side_effects.interpretation: Adrenergic support can increase dysrhythmia risk in acidemic myocardium.

treatments.context_specific_role: Organ support for the lethal shock pathway while antidotes and exposure control suppress upstream cyanide activity.

treatments.therapeutic_intent: Buffer life-threatening acidemia while antidote, ventilation, and perfusion support reduce ongoing lactate generation.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Buffering is more relevant when acidemia is severe.
Sodium and volume load require monitoring when renal reserve is poor.

side_effects.interpretation: Desired buffer effect; overshoot alkalemia and sodium load require monitoring.

treatments.context_specific_role: Bridge for severe acidemia; it stabilizes pH but does not substitute for cyanide detoxification.

treatments.therapeutic_intent: Suppress seizure excursions and secondary brain injury while antidote, oxygenation, pH, and perfusion are corrected.

sigma_modulation.clinical_rationale: Seizure treatment and neurocritical monitoring reduce physiologic variance and secondary excursions.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Seizure-directed therapy modifies seizure hazard when seizure activity or high risk is present.
Sedating antiseizure therapy can interact with airway protection needs.

side_effects.interpretation: Sedating antiseizure drugs can worsen airway or ventilation risk without monitoring.

treatments.context_specific_role: Controls a secondary injury pathway while cyanide-specific therapy and resuscitation address upstream mechanisms.

treatments.display_name: Renal replacement support for thiocyanate or refractory acid-base context
treatments.therapeutic_intent: Support clearance and acid-base control when thiocyanate accumulation, renal failure, or refractory acidemia complicates cyanide/nitroprusside physiology.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Thiocyanate accumulation is a clearance indication context.
Persistent severe acidemia may require extracorporeal support when standard measures fail.

side_effects.interpretation: Extracorporeal therapy can worsen hypotension depending on modality and volume status.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct for clearance and acid-base complications, most relevant to nitroprusside/thiocyanate or renal failure contexts.

Untreated histotoxic hypoxia increases brain injury risk.
Delayed reversal increases completed injury.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: Binding cyanide is less outcome-changing after irreversible injury or prolonged arrest.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises ongoing cyanide generation and thiocyanate accumulation risk, especially with renal or hepatic dysfunction.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Nitroprusside context is the observed exposure route.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: Stopping the infusion removes ongoing cyanide generation.
Sulfur donor support can increase detoxification of nitroprusside-derived cyanide.

present.trajectory_modulation: Reduces thiocyanate clearance and complicates sodium thiosulfate or nitroprusside-related courses.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Low renal clearance is the key observable risk context.
Thiocyanate clearance is renal.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: Extracorporeal support becomes more relevant when clearance is impaired.

present.trajectory_modulation: Can reduce endogenous rhodanese/thiosulfate detoxification reserve for a given exposure.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Impaired detoxification allows mitochondrial inhibition to persist longer.
Reduced detox reserve increases hazard for the same exposure.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: Sulfur donor provision is more relevant when endogenous reserve is low.

present.trajectory_modulation: Lowers tolerance for histotoxic hypoxia, methemoglobinemia, CO coexposure, shock, and dysrhythmia.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Baseline cardiac disease increases rhythm vulnerability during acidosis and hypoxia.
Lower oxygen reserve makes methemoglobin induction less tolerable.
Reduced reserve raises hazard for the same toxic field.

present.trajectory_modulation: Maternal hypoxia, shock, and antidote context carry fetal oxygen-delivery implications; pregnancy also lowers tolerance for avoidable oxygen-carrying-capacity loss.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Therapeutic methemoglobinemia may reduce maternal-fetal oxygen delivery reserve.
Pregnancy changes oxygen reserve and monitoring stakes, but maternal survival is still governed by the same mechanisms.

present.trajectory_modulation: Lower physiologic reserve and smaller exposure margins can speed decompensation and complicate history.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Small airway reserve, coma, or smoke injury can decompensate rapidly.
Lower physiologic reserve increases outcome hazard.

risk_factors.clinical_rationale: Documented occupational sodium-cyanide exposure is high-specificity source geometry and can drive rapid coma, lactic acidosis, and cardiovascular collapse.
Documented occupational sodium-cyanide exposure is high-specificity source geometry and can drive rapid coma, lactic acidosis, and cardiovascular collapse.

supportive_care: Keep the first-layer leaf name pure: Cyanide poisoning. Do not encode smoke, fire, severe, coma, cardiac arrest, nitroprusside, or ingestion qualifiers into disease_name.

Record exposure with parent and satellite axes: cyanide_exposure_presence -> cyanide_exposure_probability, exposure intensity, timing, smoke/fire, industrial/lab, ingestion, cyanogenic/nitrile, and nitroprusside contexts.

In smoke exposure, preserve carbon monoxide and airway injury separately: carboxyhemoglobin_percent and carbon_monoxide_coexposure_probability modify oxygen reserve but do not replace the cyanide manifold.

Track serum lactate, pH, bicarbonate, anion gap, MAP, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, mental status/GCS, seizures, ECG/troponin, and event hazards serially because the disease can evolve over minutes.
When observed, high central or mixed venous oxygen saturation and low arteriovenous oxygen saturation difference should support oxygen-extraction failure rather than be treated as normal physiology.
Do not wait for blood cyanide concentration when the exposure/lactate/shock pattern is strong; blood_cyanide_concentration is a measurement axis, not a prerequisite label.

For nitrite donors, explicitly model methemoglobin_fraction, carboxyhemoglobin_percent, oxygen saturation, anemia/cardiopulmonary reserve, hypotension, and pregnancy context; do not treat nitrite chemistry as universally harmless.
For hydroxocobalamin, monitor for chromophore-related lab interference, transient hypertension, urine/skin discoloration, and compatibility with dialysis or lab workflows.
For sodium thiosulfate and nitroprusside contexts, track thiocyanate accumulation and renal impairment as treatment/context axes.
In coma, seizure, smoke inhalation, or severe acidosis, airway and ventilation support should preserve minute ventilation while antidote and perfusion support reduce ongoing lactate generation.
Post-stabilization follow-up should preserve neurologic and cardiac injury hazards rather than deleting the early toxic evidence.

notes.distillation_method: Mechanism-first disease-name-only distillation. No real case search or case-specific evidence was used.
ontology_notes: Exactly one derived_hazard axis is included: mortality_hazard_in_D-CYANIDE-POISONING.
Smoke inhalation and carbon monoxide coexposure are source/context axes; carbon monoxide poisoning remains a separate disease manifold.
Hydroxocobalamin, sodium thiosulfate, and nitrite donor therapies are represented by general V5 treatment modes and context modifiers rather than treatment-rank labels.

Parent finding plus satellite/measurement structure is explicit for cyanide exposure/source contexts, smoke context, carbon monoxide coexposure, hypotension/MAP, shock severity, altered mental status/GCS/coma, seizure severity, and smoke airway injury.
